title: Find the repeat before guessing the next shape
practice: Try a few problems at your own pace, then return to any explanation you want to revisit.

sections.html:
Lay out a round button, a square tile and another round button. Repeat the same three objects: round, square, round; round, square, round. The unit has three positions, even though two contain the same shape.

A repeating pattern uses a unit again and again. Finding the whole unit is more reliable than looking only at the last pair. Two rounds can meet where one unit ends and another begins.
sections.title: A rhythm you can point to

sections.html:
Write circle, square, circle; circle, square, circle. Cover the final shape with your hand and predict it. Then underline each complete three-position unit.

Point to the start of each repeated unit. If your proposed unit does not account for every object in your written pattern, revise it. A good explanation covers the whole example, not just the answer you want to pick.
sections.title: Try it yourself

sections.html:
Round, square, round, square repeats. A pile of one counter, then two, then three grows. Both have structure, but “repeat the same unit” explains only the first.

When a puzzle states that a repeating rule is being used, that is useful information. Without a stated rule, a short list can often be continued in several ways. In this course, activities tell you which sort of rule to examine.
sections.title: Separate a repeat from growth

sections.html:
Instead of saying only “square”, say “the two-item unit is round then square, and the next position is the square”. That makes your reasoning easy to check.

If you get a question wrong, compare your proposed rule with the earlier items. The next lesson applies the same habit to number sequences: identify a rule and test every step.
sections.title: Make the explanation part of the answer

description: Look for a complete repeating unit, check it against every item, and avoid guessing from just the last two shapes.
